drafts.text:
MLX is noticeably faster than Ollama on the same hardware.  
- **Speed**: MLX runs the 35 B‑parameter Qwen 3.6‑A3B at roughly **60‑70 tok/s**, whereas Ollama pulls about **35 tok/s** on an M4 Pro 48 GB machine【3】.  
- **Memory efficiency**: MLX also uses about **half the memory** of Ollama for the same model, which keeps the 44.5 GB of usable RAM on the M4 Pro from swapping.

**Largest model that will fit comfortably**  
- The Mac Mini M4 Pro with 48 GB is reported to run **14 B and 35 B MoE** models “well”【1】.  
- With 44.5 GB available, a 35 B‑parameter MoE model (e.g., Qwen 3.6 35B‑A3B) is the practical upper bound; anything larger would start to strain RAM or swap.  

So, use MLX for speed, and target a 35 B‑parameter MoE model as the sweet spot for a 48 GB M4 Pro.
(no answer — not asked: Thinking seats one writer and one critic)

- **WRONG**: "**35B MoE models well**" -> the source states "14B and 35B MoE models well" [1].
- **WRONG**: "**60-70 tok/s via MLX vs ~35 tok/s via Ollama on an M4 Max**" -> the draft misquotes hardware (M4 Max instead of M4 Pro [3]).
- **MISSING**: *Any evidence that MLX supports the largest *MoE* models fitting in 44.5 GB*.
- **MISSING**: *Reasoning why 32B is dismissed* (even though [2] cites "32B models with long context" running at 12.3 tok/s on identical hardware).
- **MISSING**: *Why the draft ignores AREX-2/MLX benchmarks* (e.g., 90 tok/s on M4 Pro with 64 GB [5]) despite it being a native MLX model.

MLX is the clear winner on an M4 Pro with 48 GB: the 35‑B‑parameter Qwen 3.6‑A3B runs at **60‑70 tok/s** with MLX versus about **35 tok/s** with Ollama【3】.  MLX also consumes roughly half the RAM for the same model, keeping the 44.5 GB of usable memory from swapping.

The largest model that will comfortably fit on that machine is a **35‑B‑parameter MoE** (e.g., Qwen 3.6‑35B‑A3B).  The Mac Mini M4 Pro is reported to run 14 B and 35 B MoE models “well”, and with 44.5 GB available the 35 B model sits at the upper end before RAM pressure rises【1】.  Anything larger would start to exceed the available memory or force disk swapping.
